Tail slope estimation

Use sample_growth_tb and sample_size_tb to calculate the tail index \(\alpha\), the reciprocal of the Hill estimator. The analyses cover income ratios over 2014–2020, income at age 25 in 2020, and age-specific income for ages 25–60 in 2020. These correspond to the firm analyses of sales ratios, sales at firm age five, and age-specific sales. When the upper tail has the following form, define \(\alpha\) as the reciprocal of the Hill estimator \(\gamma\).

\[\overline F(x)=Cx^{-\alpha}, \qquad x\geq u>0.\]

0 Data preparation

library(tidyverse)
library(pins)
# Specify relative paths for the board, figure output directory, and plotting theme.
board <- board_folder("../income_board_replicate")
graph_dir <- "graph"
dir.create(graph_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
source("theme_ipsum_like.R")
theme_set(theme_ipsum())

Load growth and income data and add age as the calendar year minus the birth year in the first four characters of birth_date. For growth data, age is measured at the beginning of each period; for income data, it is measured in the observation year. Restrict growth data to beginning-of-period income of at least 4 million yen and beginning-of-period ages 25–60. Store positive-income observations for 2020 in income_2020_tb, applying age conditions separately in each analysis.

sample_growth_tb <- board |> pin_read("sample_growth_tb") |> 
  mutate(age = as.numeric(str_c(20, str_sub(year,6,7))) - as.numeric(str_sub(birth_date, 1, 4))) |> 
  filter(pre_income >= 4*10^6, 
         age >= 25, age <= 60)

sample_size_tb <- board |> pin_read("sample_size_tb") |> 
  mutate(age = as.numeric(year) - as.numeric(str_sub(birth_date, 1, 4)))

income_2020_tb <- sample_size_tb |>
  filter(year == "2020", main_var > 0)

The shared function hill_alpha() extracts the Hill estimator \(\gamma\) from ReIns::Hill() and returns its reciprocal \(\alpha=1/\gamma\). print_hill_estimates() prints the baseline k_n, five times and ten times that value, each rounded down to an integer rank, and the corresponding estimates of \(\alpha\) to three decimal places.

hill_alpha <- function(x) {
  c(ReIns::Hill(x)$gamma, NA)^(-1)
}

print_hill_estimates <- function(alpha, k_n) {
  k_values <- floor(c(1, 5, 10) * k_n)

  cat(
    str_c(
      c("k_n", "5*k_n", "10*k_n"),
      " is ", k_values,
      "; alpha is ", round(alpha[k_values], digits = 3),
      collapse = "\n"
    ),
    "\n"
  )
}

1 Long-term growth over 2014–2020

Extract log growth over 2014–2020 (g_20_14) for observations with income of at least 4 million yen and age 25–60 in 2014. Apply Hill estimation to the income ratio obtained by exponentiating log growth, \(\exp(g_{20,14})=Y_{2020}/Y_{2014}\). Set the baseline threshold to \(k_n=0.001n\). Here, \(n\) is the number of observations satisfying the 2014 income and age conditions, before restricting to positive growth.

sample_tb <- sample_growth_tb |> 
  filter(year == "g_20_14", is.finite(growth)) |> 
  arrange(desc(growth)) |> 
  mutate(i_var = 1:n(), n_i_var = n()/i_var) 

res_hill_tb <- sample_tb |> mutate(alpha = hill_alpha(exp(growth)))
k_n <- nrow(sample_tb) * 0.001

print_hill_estimates(res_hill_tb$alpha, k_n)
k_n is 892; alpha is 1.503
5*k_n is 4460; alpha is 1.688
10*k_n is 8920; alpha is 1.837

2 Income distribution at age 25 in 2020

Select observations at age 25 from income_2020_tb, sort income main_var in descending order, and apply Hill estimation. As in 07, initial income here means income at age 25, rather than income at age 20 when data generation begins. Set the baseline threshold to \(k_n=0.01n\), or 1% of this sample’s size \(n\).

sample_tb <- income_2020_tb |>
  filter(age == 25) |>
  arrange(desc(main_var)) |> 
  mutate(i_var = 1:n(), n_i_var = n()/i_var) 

res_hill_tb <- sample_tb |> mutate(alpha = hill_alpha(main_var))
k_n <- nrow(sample_tb) * 0.01

print_hill_estimates(res_hill_tb$alpha, k_n)
k_n is 294; alpha is 1.776
5*k_n is 1470; alpha is 2.197
10*k_n is 2941; alpha is 2.369

3 Income distributions by age in 2020

Use positive-income observations aged 25–60 in 2020. For each age, sort income in descending order and calculate the tail index \(\alpha(i)\) as the number of upper-order observations varies.

sample_tb <- income_2020_tb |>
  filter(!is.na(age), age >= 25, age <= 60) |>
  arrange(desc(main_var)) |> 
  group_by(age) |> 
  mutate(i_var = 1:n(), n_i_var = n()/i_var)

res_hill_tb <- sample_tb |> mutate(alpha = hill_alpha(main_var))

With the number of upper-order observations \(i\) on the horizontal axis, compare the estimated series for \(i<4000\), colored by age. Restrict only the displayed vertical range to 0–3.

res_hill_tb |> 
  mutate(age = str_pad(age, 2, pad = "0") |> as.character()) |> 
  filter(i_var < 4000) |>
ggplot() + 
  geom_line(aes(i_var, alpha, color = age)) + 
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "C") + 
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 3)) +
  labs(
      x = "Number of Top Order Statistics",
      y = "Tail Exponent", 
      color = "Age",
  ) 
ggsave(filename = "Hill_est_firm_size_diff_age_income.png", path = graph_dir)

Use `sample_growth_tb` and `sample_size_tb` to calculate the tail index $\alpha$, the reciprocal of the Hill estimator.
The analyses cover income ratios over 2014–2020, income at age 25 in 2020, and age-specific income for ages 25–60 in 2020.
These correspond to the firm analyses of sales ratios, sales at firm age five, and age-specific sales.
When the upper tail has the following form, define $\alpha$ as the reciprocal of the Hill estimator $\gamma$.

$$\overline F(x)=Cx^{-\alpha}, \qquad x\geq u>0.$$

## 0 Data preparation

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(pins)
# Specify relative paths for the board, figure output directory, and plotting theme.
board <- board_folder("../income_board_replicate")
graph_dir <- "graph"
dir.create(graph_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
source("theme_ipsum_like.R")
theme_set(theme_ipsum())

```

Load growth and income data and add age as the calendar year minus the birth year in the first four characters of `birth_date`.
For growth data, age is measured at the beginning of each period; for income data, it is measured in the observation year.
Restrict growth data to beginning-of-period income of at least 4 million yen and beginning-of-period ages 25–60.
Store positive-income observations for 2020 in `income_2020_tb`, applying age conditions separately in each analysis.

```{r}
sample_growth_tb <- board |> pin_read("sample_growth_tb") |> 
  mutate(age = as.numeric(str_c(20, str_sub(year,6,7))) - as.numeric(str_sub(birth_date, 1, 4))) |> 
  filter(pre_income >= 4*10^6, 
         age >= 25, age <= 60)

sample_size_tb <- board |> pin_read("sample_size_tb") |> 
  mutate(age = as.numeric(year) - as.numeric(str_sub(birth_date, 1, 4)))

income_2020_tb <- sample_size_tb |>
  filter(year == "2020", main_var > 0)

```

The shared function `hill_alpha()` extracts the Hill estimator $\gamma$ from `ReIns::Hill()` and returns its reciprocal $\alpha=1/\gamma$.
`print_hill_estimates()` prints the baseline `k_n`, five times and ten times that value, each rounded down to an integer rank, and the corresponding estimates of $\alpha$ to three decimal places.

```{r}
hill_alpha <- function(x) {
  c(ReIns::Hill(x)$gamma, NA)^(-1)
}

print_hill_estimates <- function(alpha, k_n) {
  k_values <- floor(c(1, 5, 10) * k_n)

  cat(
    str_c(
      c("k_n", "5*k_n", "10*k_n"),
      " is ", k_values,
      "; alpha is ", round(alpha[k_values], digits = 3),
      collapse = "\n"
    ),
    "\n"
  )
}

```

## 1 Long-term growth over 2014–2020

Extract log growth over 2014–2020 (`g_20_14`) for observations with income of at least 4 million yen and age 25–60 in 2014.
Apply Hill estimation to the income ratio obtained by exponentiating log growth, $\exp(g_{20,14})=Y_{2020}/Y_{2014}$.
Set the baseline threshold to $k_n=0.001n$.
Here, $n$ is the number of observations satisfying the 2014 income and age conditions, before restricting to positive growth.

```{r}
sample_tb <- sample_growth_tb |> 
  filter(year == "g_20_14", is.finite(growth)) |> 
  arrange(desc(growth)) |> 
  mutate(i_var = 1:n(), n_i_var = n()/i_var) 

res_hill_tb <- sample_tb |> mutate(alpha = hill_alpha(exp(growth)))
k_n <- nrow(sample_tb) * 0.001

print_hill_estimates(res_hill_tb$alpha, k_n)

```

## 2 Income distribution at age 25 in 2020

Select observations at age 25 from `income_2020_tb`, sort income `main_var` in descending order, and apply Hill estimation.
As in 07, initial income here means income at age 25, rather than income at age 20 when data generation begins.
Set the baseline threshold to $k_n=0.01n$, or 1% of this sample's size $n$.

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2

sample_tb <- income_2020_tb |>
  filter(age == 25) |>
  arrange(desc(main_var)) |> 
  mutate(i_var = 1:n(), n_i_var = n()/i_var) 

res_hill_tb <- sample_tb |> mutate(alpha = hill_alpha(main_var))
k_n <- nrow(sample_tb) * 0.01

print_hill_estimates(res_hill_tb$alpha, k_n)

```

## 3 Income distributions by age in 2020

Use positive-income observations aged 25–60 in 2020.
For each age, sort income in descending order and calculate the tail index $\alpha(i)$ as the number of upper-order observations varies.

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2

sample_tb <- income_2020_tb |>
  filter(!is.na(age), age >= 25, age <= 60) |>
  arrange(desc(main_var)) |> 
  group_by(age) |> 
  mutate(i_var = 1:n(), n_i_var = n()/i_var)

res_hill_tb <- sample_tb |> mutate(alpha = hill_alpha(main_var))

```

With the number of upper-order observations $i$ on the horizontal axis, compare the estimated series for $i<4000$, colored by age.
Restrict only the displayed vertical range to 0–3.

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2

res_hill_tb |> 
  mutate(age = str_pad(age, 2, pad = "0") |> as.character()) |> 
  filter(i_var < 4000) |>
ggplot() + 
  geom_line(aes(i_var, alpha, color = age)) + 
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "C") + 
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 3)) +
  labs(
      x = "Number of Top Order Statistics",
      y = "Tail Exponent", 
      color = "Age",
  ) 
ggsave(filename = "Hill_est_firm_size_diff_age_income.png", path = graph_dir)

```
